extracted.intended_audience: science and health journalists (writers and editors) seeking guidance on transgender-inclusive reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and reporting in science and health journalism that treats transgender people respectfully, avoids exclusionary assumptions, and improves coverage and sourcing. Covers interviewing, language usage, sourcing, newsroom practices, and when to use sensitivity readers or trans experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat trans sources with professionalism and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat transgender people the same way you would treat anyone else while being sensitive to potentially intrusive subjects such as transitioning or harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reassure sources they don't have to answer intrusive questions and seek consent before asking sensitive questions. Bring dignity to interviews and avoid treating trans people as curiosities; the same standards of professionalism apply as with cisgender sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask preferred terminology for body parts early
rubrics_metrics.description: At the start of interviews, ask what language a person uses to describe relevant body parts or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a trans man who hasn't had top surgery might prefer 'chest' instead of 'breasts.' Say something like, 'If I say a term that makes you uncomfortable, please let me know. And let me know which term you would like to be used so that you feel safe.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Never deadname except very limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use a trans person’s former name (deadname). The only acceptable exceptions are rare circumstances such as a quoted use by the source with permission or immediate coverage of a celebrity’s recent name change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If quoting a source who uses their former name, replace it in brackets with their correct name. For celebrities, avoid deadnaming by describing them (e.g., 'an Olympic decathlete and Kris Jenner’s former spouse'); if identity is unclear, mention the old name once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false balance and refuse to legitimize anti-trans perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give undue legitimacy to anti-trans viewpoints that lack scientific grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from seeking out token anti-trans commentators to 'balance' stories; avoid overemphasizing detransitioning, which is rare and often sensationalized. Prefer trans experts and sources when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize transgender voices as authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat trans people as authorities on their own experiences and seek trans experts for trans-related topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you need an expert on a trans health matter, look for one who is trans. Interview trans kids and adults when reporting on topics that affect them (e.g., puberty blockers) rather than relying only on cisgender parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider assigning trans journalists to trans-related stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, recommend or assign understaffed trans journalists to cover stories about trans bodies and communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cis reporters should consider recommending trans reporters for trans-related assignments because trans reporters can be more accurate, nuanced, and have better access and rapport with sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trans-focused style guides but defer to individual preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult style guides (Trans Journalists Association, Association of LGBTQ Journalists, GLAAD, Radical Copyeditor) for consensus terminology, but always defer to how an individual source wants to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style guides evolve and may conflict—use them as a starting point and cross-check options. No one expects perfect knowledge; be humble and ask for help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclusionary phrasing like 'he or she'; use singular 'they'
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace binary phrasing such as 'he or she' with singular 'they' and avoid gendering an unspecified person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid gendering groups (e.g., 'men and women') unless you know everyone in the group identifies that way. Use neutral or specific language (e.g., 'people who menstruate') where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use the phrase 'preferred pronouns'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid saying 'preferred pronouns' because it implies correct pronouns are optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for and use the pronouns a person requests. Examples of neopronouns (ze/hir, ey/em) should be respected even if unfamiliar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get names and pronouns at the start of interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask sources for their names and pronouns at the outset so you can use them correctly in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to use unfamiliar pronouns and respect them. Do not treat pronoun disclosure as optional or as a conversational novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful when mentioning a source's trans identity; only when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not call out a trans person's gender identity unless it's relevant to the story's context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In stories about trans matters it's often appropriate to identify that a source is trans to establish authority; for unrelated stories avoid referencing gender identity. When in doubt, consult a sensitivity reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid phrasing like 'identifies as'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid wording such as 'X identifies as non-binary' because it can imply the gender is less valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct statements (e.g., 'X is non-binary') or whatever phrasing the source prefers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate anatomy with gender identity in health reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid assuming anatomy and gender match or using anatomy as shorthand for gender (e.g., saying 'women' when discussing menstruation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about what you mean (body parts, processes, or populations). Use terms like 'people who menstruate' or refer directly to the body part or process to be accurate and inclusive; once established, you can use shorter pronouns like 'people.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how researchers categorize sex and gender in studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether research conflates sex and gender or lumps different populations together in a way that muddies conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate study methodologies (e.g., grouping 'men who have sex with men' with transgender women) and report how categorization choices affect data validity and relevance for trans populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and highlight research gaps about trans people
rubrics_metrics.description: If research on how a topic affects trans people is missing, explicitly say so and highlight those gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing out gaps can push researchers to study marginalized communities and inform readers about limits of existing knowledge (example: lack of research on sexual dysfunction in non-binary or trans people).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek consent before intrusive questions and offer opt-out
rubrics_metrics.description: When asking about sensitive topics (transitioning, harassment), ask for consent and remind sources they don't have to answer uncomfortable questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit language: 'You do not have to answer this. Feel free to tell me if you are uncomfortable.' This approach reduces harm and builds trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire and pay sensitivity readers/consultants when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sensitivity readers or consultants for potentially exclusionary content and be prepared to compensate them for emotional labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure about trans-inclusive language or context, hire a sensitivity reader (examples: Race and Gender Hotline, trans-led consulting companies) and respect refusals. Paying for time helps avoid unpaid labor burdens on trans people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand emotional labor from trans peers; accept refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about repeatedly asking trans colleagues or peers to educate you; their time and emotional labor are not owed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask politely, be willing to take no for an answer, and, when possible, pay for consultative work rather than expecting unpaid help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call out anti-trans remarks and foster newsroom accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Address anti-trans jokes or comments in the workplace and hold colleagues accountable to create a safer environment for trans staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervene by naming problematic language (e.g., 'that was problematic') and explain why. Creating accountability helps retain and respect trans journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful when introducing neopronouns; decide whether to explain
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no consensus on introducing neopronouns; some recommend a brief explanatory aside while others find it alienating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adding an explanation, keep it short and accessible (example: 'Taylor, who uses ze/hir pronouns, attended the event'). Balance audience comprehension with not othering the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use efficient inclusive phrasing and push back on editors when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose concise, inclusive language (e.g., 'people with prostates') to maintain readability and accuracy, and advocate for inclusive wording with editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freelancers may have less leverage—allies should speak up on their behalf. Tight phrasing can make inclusive language easier to approve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult trans-led resources and organizations for guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use resources like the Trans Journalists Association, Association of LGBTQ Journalists' stylebook, GLAAD Media Reference Guide, and Radical Copyeditor's guide for terminology and evolving consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check guides for conflicts, and use them as starting points; remember that community preferences evolve quickly and individual preference overrides guide recommendations.
